subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: Structure 1.1 — Particulate nature of matter (Sep unit)

cards.back: Substance made of only one type of atom; cannot be broken down by chemical means.
Two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Its properties differ from those of its elements.
Two or more substances not chemically bonded, in any ratio; components keep their properties and can be separated physically.
Homogeneous: uniform composition, one phase (salt water, air). Heterogeneous: non-uniform, visibly separate phases (sand in water, oil and water).

cards.front: Separate an insoluble solid from a liquid
cards.back: Filtration: the solid stays as residue, the liquid passes through as filtrate.

cards.front: Recover a dissolved solid from a solution
cards.back: Evaporation, or crystallisation/recrystallisation (concentrate, cool, collect crystals) for a purer product.

cards.front: Separate salt from a sand–salt mixture
cards.back: Add water to dissolve (solvation) the salt, filter off the sand, then evaporate or crystallise the salt from the filtrate.
Distillation (fractional distillation if boiling points are close): the lower-boiling liquid vaporises first and is condensed and collected.

cards.front: What separates the components of an ink?
cards.back: Paper chromatography: components travel different distances depending on their relative attraction to the solvent (mobile phase) and the paper (stationary phase).

cards.front: Solid, liquid and gas in the kinetic molecular model
cards.back: Solid: particles vibrate about fixed positions. Liquid: close together but can move past each other. Gas: far apart, moving fast and randomly; attractions negligible.
s→l melting, l→s freezing, l→g vaporisation (evaporation or boiling), g→l condensation, s→g sublimation, g→s deposition.
Evaporation: only at the surface, at any temperature below the boiling point. Boiling: throughout the liquid, at the boiling point.
(s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. Include them in equations when asked.
Temperature in kelvin is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles.
T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15. A change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C. Example: 25 °C = 298.15 K (298 K).
0 K (−273.15 °C): the lowest possible temperature, where particle kinetic energy is at a minimum.

cards.front: Why is the temperature constant during a change of state on a heating curve?
cards.back: The energy supplied overcomes attractions between particles (increases potential energy), not their average kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.

cards.front: Heating curve of ice to steam: which flat section is longer, and why?
cards.back: Boiling (l→g) takes longer than melting, because separating particles completely needs much more energy than loosening them from a lattice.
